dct_description_sm: Recent green house effect scenarios predict a significant warming of the atmosphere over north-eastern Canada. Regional climate models further show a particularly important warming during winter over Hudson Bay, a large inland sea (about one million square kilometers). The impact of such warming may include the thinning and gradual disappearance of the seasonal ice cover, with direct consequences over polar bears, seals, and the sea ice algae component of the primary production. Hudson Bay is also a large-scale estuarine system because of the important discharge of freshwater from rivers (about 800 cubic kilometers per year). This freshwater source along with the wind regime define the mean circulation of the waters. The reduced sea ice cover in a warmer climate may modify the stratification and the momentum input from winds, resulting in a modified circulation pattern, and changes in the water masses' characteristics. Furthermore, the fresh outflow from Hudson Bay and Hudson Strait represents a signficant freshwater contribution to the Labrador Sea, a well-known location for dense water formation. The freshwater outflow from Hudson Bay and Hudson Strait may then play a role in the global ocean's circulation and variability. The MERICA missions were planned to enhance our understanding of the system and to closely follow its evolution over time.
dct_title_s: Survey and study of Hudson Bay's climate
